jukan-rtx50-korea-price-hike-memory-cost:
Prices for NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 50 series in South Korea rise by up to 30% starting this month.
What pushed them up is not a performance upgrade or a new launch. It is component cost.

@@REF@@GeForce RTX 50 Prices Could Jump Another 30% as Memory Crunch Deepens (ThinkComputers, 2026-07-31)|https://thinkcomputers.org/geforce-rtx-50-prices-could-jump-another-30-as-memory-crunch-deepens|https://thinkcomputers.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/rtx-5080-2025-1.webp

That report shows this is not only a Korean story.
It says NVIDIA may raise graphics card prices by a further 20 to 30% during 2026, with the increase landing in the weeks or months after partner inventory sells through.
Korea's increase this month looks like the same schedule arriving early.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/NVIDIA_GPU.jpg/960px-NVIDIA_GPU.jpg|A graphics card. The large chip in the middle is the graphics processor, and the smaller chips ringing it are the memory that just got more expensive.|Mickael Courtiade · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NVIDIA_GPU.jpg

## Why is there memory on a graphics card
A graphics processor has to pull the data it draws with at very high speed.
So the board carries several dedicated memory chips around the processor, and that memory is called GDDR.

It shares its roots with the DRAM you plug into a desktop.
The design is simply tilted toward moving a lot of data at once.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg/960px-DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg|A DRAM stick for a desktop. The GDDR on a graphics card comes off the same production lines, which is why it moves with DRAM prices.|Smial · FAL 1.3|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DDR5_SDRAM_(with_scale)_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg

Same process, same fabs. That is the heart of what is happening.
When a memory maker gives more of its lines to server parts, the volume headed for gaming parts shrinks, and what is left gets repriced.

## How much more expensive

@@CHK@@GDDR7 3GB module|$60 to $70|GDDR6 2GB module|about $20|Per gigabyte|about $22 for GDDR7 against about $10 for GDDR6@@The GDDR7 used by the RTX 50 series costs roughly twice as much per gigabyte as the previous generation. Several of these modules sit on a single card, so doubling the module price enlarges memory's share of the card's cost by the same order.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03, citing ThinkComputers (2026-07-31), originally sourced to Economic Daily News

What rose here is not the price of a finished card but the price of one part inside it.
Same model, same performance, different price tag.

## Who raised the price
NVIDIA sells few finished cards itself. It hands board makers a kit that bundles the graphics processor with the memory.
It has reportedly told those partners that the kit price is going up.

@@REF@@NVIDIA is reportedly increasing the prices of its GeForce RTX GPUs due to rising memory costs (TweakTown, 2026-07-23)|https://www.tweaktown.com/news/112801/nvidia-is-reportedly-increasing-the-prices-of-its-geforce-rtx-gpus-due-to-rising-memory-costs/index.html|https://static.tweaktown.com/news/1/1/112801_2_nvidia-is-reportedly-increasing-the-prices-of-its-geforce-rtx-gpus-due-to-rising-memory-costs_full.jpg

That report adds that the increase covers not only the GDDR7-based RTX 50 series but the older GDDR6-based RTX 3060.
So this is not a charge attached to new products. It is attached to any card that uses memory.
Cooling parts and boards are said to have become more expensive as well.

## Who really sets this price
It starts with where a memory maker points its lines.
As long as server DRAM and HBM keep selling for more, gaming GDDR waits its turn.

So a graphics card's price follows the direction of memory prices more closely than it follows NVIDIA's pricing policy.
The shopper sees a price tag on a card, but the hand moving that tag is at a memory supply negotiation.

## What settles it
The question comes down to one thing. Is this increase a price that comes back down once the crunch eases, or one that settles in.

If output from the capacity memory makers have added starts arriving and server demand takes a breather, the first reading is right.
If the added output keeps going to server customers first, gaming card prices stay where they have moved to.

The AI build-out is usually discussed in units of data centres and power.
One of the earliest points where that spending reaches a household budget is this month's graphics card price tag.
macro-week-2026-08-02:
Eight numbers from last week's Kobeissi Letter, lined up in a row.
Apart they are separate stories. Side by side they point the same way.

Global household net worth reached a record $570 trillion in 2025, up 7.3% in a year.
Equities produced 57% of that increase, real estate just 15%.

@@CHK@@Global household net worth (2025)|$570 trillion|Share of the increase from equities|57%|Share from real capital formation|20%@@The $570 trillion is $40 trillion more than a year earlier. McKinsey writes that only 20% of that increase came from actually building anything, while close to 60% came from asset prices rising faster than inflation. Between 2000 and 2024 real estate produced more than half of wealth growth. Last year equities took that place.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · McKinsey Global Institute, The Global Balance Sheet 2026 (published 2026-07-23, 2025 data)

@@REF@@The global balance sheet 2026: Imbalance and divergence (McKinsey Global Institute, 2026-07-23)|https://www.mckinsey.com/mgi/our-research/the-global-balance-sheet-2026-imbalance-and-divergence|https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/mckinsey%20global%20institute/our%20research/the%20global%20balance%20sheet%202026%20imbalance%20and%20divergence/the%20global%20balance%20sheet%202026-1002127418-medium-thumb-1536x1536.jpg

The same report puts the entire global balance sheet near $1.8 quadrillion.
Put simply, the world got richer last year not by making more things, but because the things it already owned were marked higher.

## Who did that wealth land on

If equities made the wealth, it landed on whoever holds equities.
The top 1% of US earners own 50.1% of US stocks and mutual funds, up from 40.1% in 1990.
The bottom half of earners own 1.1%.

Across investors as a whole the tilt is also at a record.
Equities are 65% of the assets held by US households, pension funds, insurers and funds, eight percentage points above the dot-com peak.

## Meanwhile the support underneath is thinning

The rest of the week's numbers run the other way.

The US personal saving rate fell to 2.7% in June, the lowest since June 2022 and a fifth straight monthly decline.
The 2014 to 2019 average was 5.5%. Assets grew while the share of income households keep halved.

Borrowed money is shrinking too.
Margin debt across Korea, China and Taiwan is down $67 billion from its June peak.
Korean leveraged ETFs tied to SK Hynix and Samsung have lost 63% of their assets.

@@REF@@Korea's Leveraged Chip Trade Hits the Margin Call Wall (Investing.com, 2026-07-16)|https://www.investing.com/analysis/koreas-leveraged-chip-trade-hits-the-margin-call-wall-200684082|https://i-invdn-com.investing.com/redesign/images/seo/investingcom_analysis_og.jpg

That analysis reports margin calls on 1.2 million leveraged retail accounts by July 13, with 320,000 to 360,000 liquidated outright.
The leverage came down closer to being forced out by falling prices than to investors changing their minds.

Hedge funds moved the same way, selling global tech stocks over three days into July 28 at the fastest pace since records began in 2016.

## Which way is the price of money going

The last two numbers are close to the answer.

The market puts a record 60% probability on a quarter-point hike at the September FOMC. A hike, not a cut.
Central banks bought a net 289 tonnes of gold in the second quarter, 62 tonnes more than a year earlier and the largest quarterly addition since Q4 2024.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Gold_bullion_bars.jpg/960px-Gold_bullion_bars.jpg|Gold bars. Central banks added 289 tonnes in a single quarter, an asset sitting on the opposite side of price-driven wealth.|Stevebidmead · CC0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gold_bullion_bars.jpg

Borrowing is being priced to get more expensive, and central banks are stacking the one asset that does not depend on a market marking it up.

## So what settles this

The question comes down to one thing.
Is last year's $570 trillion wealth that asset prices can keep producing, or wealth on paper that a single round trip in prices erases.

The place to look is the saving rate and margin balances.
If saving rises and margin debt rebuilds while prices are depressed, households absorbed the assets with their own money.
If saving stays near 2% while margin debt keeps falling, both sources of support left at once.

Wealth rising and money rising are not the same sentence.
A fifth of last year's $570 trillion was newly created. The rest was price.
meru-china-duv-ssa800-1950i-class:
The immersion scanner China says it has built sits at the same level as the NXT:1950i, a tool ASML released in 2008.
It prints 28nm circuits in a single exposure, and the generation above it, the 2015 model 1980Di, is still out of reach.

When a state-backed firm in Shanghai was reported on July 27 to have started volume production of the tool, ASML shares closed down 5.7% and fell as much as 7% intraday.

@@REF@@China begins mass production of homegrown immersion DUV machines, first units to SMIC, Hua Hong and CXMT this year (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-27)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/semiconductors/china-begins-mass-production-of-domestic-immersion-duv-lithography-machines|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/7ZotSVaMnrDA7FNSEBa4BN-970-80.jpg

Tom's Hardware reports the tool prints 28nm-class features in one exposure and reaches 7nm-class when exposures are layered on top of each other.
Deliveries run to about five units this year and roughly 20 next year.

## Why a 2008 model of all things

A scanner is the machine that writes circuits onto a wafer with light.
That single step eats 60% of the time and 35% of the cost of making a chip.

Start with the light itself. The domestic source built by Keyihongyuan runs at 6kHz and 60W.
ASML's part delivers 90W at the same frequency.

For the optics, Maolai is said to have passed validation on a 300mm large-aperture lens.
Its precision lands around 30nm, against under 10nm for Germany's ZEISS lenses, so ZEISS lenses were reportedly imported in the end.

@@REF@@China's DUV lithography still lags ASML by four generations (Asia Times, 2026-07-31)|https://asiatimes.com/2026/07/chinas-duv-lithography-still-lags-asml-by-four-generations/|https://asiatimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/SSA800.jpg

Asia Times names the tool the SSA800 and reports it was built by Shanghai Aishengna Electronic Technology Group, founded in 2023, which absorbed development teams from Yuliangsheng and SMEE.
Roughly 70% of the parts are domestic, while mirrors for the 193nm excimer laser, ZEISS lenses, vacuum chambers and synchronization control algorithms are still imported.
Turn that 70% around and it says 30% has to be bought from outside before the machine can be built at all.

## Why the 1980Di could not be copied

Huawei already held the generation above.
HSMC in Wuhan brought in an ASML 1980Di for a 7nm fab and then went bankrupt, and the Chinese government took over the company and handed it to Huawei.

In October 2025, China asked ASML to repair that machine.
The engineer who went on site reportedly found it taken apart and never put back together.

Calibration is what stands in the way.
It is a precision setting that aligns the lenses, mirrors and wafer stage down to the nanometer, fixed at the factory over weeks against hundreds of reference points.
Opening the machine throws that alignment off, and the software key that restores it sits only with ASML.

Even holding the finished product, you lose it the moment you look inside.

## What ASML actually stands to lose

China moved fast because of the calendar.
EUV was blocked from 2019, the NXT:2000i and above from late 2023, and the 1970i and 1980i from September 2024.
Ninety units of the 1980i were stockpiled just before the rules landed, but servicing that lifts performance by more than 1% was banned too, which made upkeep hard.

@@CHK@@ASML China share of sales, H1 2026|about 16%|ASML Q2 2026 net sales|EUR 9.3bn|ASML Q2 2026 net income|EUR 2.9bn@@The market China wants to win back with a domestic tool has already shrunk to about a sixth of ASML's sales. Export controls cut that share first, so what ASML newly loses if localization works is smaller by the same amount. The number points the same way the author does.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · sales and net income from ASML's Q2 2026 results release, China share as reported by Tech Wire Asia

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether this is the first crack in ASML's moat, or a detour that export controls forced open.

The generation is what settles it.
While the tool stays at 1950i class, it is a detour.
The moment a 1980Di-class machine comes out of domestic parts alone, it is a crack.

ASML took seven years to move from 28nm to 7nm.
There is no visible reason the side walking that road again on a domestic light source and domestic lenses gets less time than that.
A scanner is the one seat in the chip supply chain with no substitute, and whoever holds it is what gives export controls their leverage.
That this tool sits at 2008 level says the leverage is still there.
meru-us-japan-joint-yen-intervention-esf:
On July 31 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York sold euros and bought yen on behalf of the US Treasury. It is the first time since 2011, fifteen years, that the United States has entered the currency market on the buying side of the yen.

Bloomberg reported that Japan alone spent 8.45 trillion yen, about $52.8 billion, on July 30, the day before. Observers put that at the largest single day Tokyo has ever spent. The yen closed Friday at 157.40 to the dollar, its strongest since early May.

What the United States added is less than a fifth of that. What will make this intervention worth remembering is not the amount but the way the dollars were made.

## A single memo caught in a Reuters photo

It started with one piece of paper.

On July 31 a Reuters photograph from a cabinet meeting caught Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's memo in full. Under the words 'to do' was the line 'buy $5-10bn of yen'. Reuters reported that the Treasury had warned banks that morning that an intervention was possible. The Treasury did not respond on the contents of the memo.

That there was neither a denial nor a confirmation read, in the market, as confirmation.

## To buy yen you first need dollars

Making the yen stronger means selling dollars and buying yen. That requires having the dollars first, and where those dollars come from is the heart of this episode.

The money Japan uses on the exchange rate comes from the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account run by the Ministry of Finance. It holds about $1.3747 trillion, and $1.0087 trillion of that, most of what can be turned into cash immediately, is US Treasuries. Japan's dollar wallet is filled with Treasuries. Opening the wallet means selling them, and the moment they are sold the market has more of them, prices fall and yields rise.

And the indicator Bessent has repeatedly said he watches most closely is the 10-year Treasury yield.

Selling Treasuries to hold up the yen pushes US yields up. That is the problem this intervention had to solve first.

## The ESF and FIMA, two wallets that leave Treasuries alone

What the United States sold this time was not dollars but euros.

The Treasury keeps a separate pocket called the Exchange Stabilization Fund, and it holds euros and yen. Selling euros to buy yen touches not a single Treasury.

What Japan will use is not yet confirmed. The original post expects Japan to use the FIMA repo facility. Created in March 2020, it lets a central bank pledge the Treasuries it already keeps at the New York Fed as collateral, borrow dollars for a while and buy them back later.

@@REF@@Federal Reserve announces the establishment of a standing FIMA repo facility (Federal Reserve, 2021-07-28)|https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20210728b.htm|https://www.federalreserve.gov/images/social-media/social-default-image-opengraph.jpg

The Fed's announcement pins the collateral to Treasuries held in custody at the New York Fed and the per-country limit to $60 billion. Selling a Treasury and pledging one are entirely different things in the market. Selling puts the paper on the market; pledging does not.

## $52.8bn in a day against a $60bn window

Japan spent $52.8 billion in a single day on July 30. The per-country limit on FIMA repo is $60 billion.

Drawing the window once, all the way, barely covers one of those days. For this facility to be a way of holding on without selling Treasuries, it has to be borrowed and repaid over and over, and the dollars for repayment have to come from somewhere in the end. Pledging as collateral may not remove Treasury selling so much as push it back.

If the yen turns on its own inside the time bought, it ends as time bought. If it does not, it arrives all at once, in proportion to the delay.

## The single line that prints on Thursday, August 6

The Fed publishes its balance sheet every Thursday. One line on it records the dollars foreign monetary authorities have borrowed against Treasuries. That line reads zero right now.

If a number other than zero prints on August 6, Japan found its dollars without selling Treasuries. If it stays at zero while the yen slips again, Japan went back to the old method or stopped intervening.

Where the yen goes from 157 will be in the news all week. Nobody will write up that one line on Thursday. It is the second of the two that will still be there in a few years.
schiff-us-credit-card-delinquency-level-:
The share of US credit card debt more than 90 days past due was 7.1% in the first quarter of 2026.
It has barely moved through five quarters in the low sevens, and it sits below the 7.2% of the fourth quarter of 2024.

@@REF@@Household debt balances rise slightly as delinquency transition rates hold steady (Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 2026-05-12)|https://www.newyorkfed.org/newsevents/news/research/2026/20260512

@@CHK@@Q1 2026|7.1%|One year earlier (Q1 2025)|7.0%|Prior peak (Q4 2024)|7.2%@@On level, Schiff is right. Outside the years right after the financial crisis it has not been this high. On direction he is not. The reading has been flat for five quarters and is below where it stood a year and a half ago. The claim that things are getting worse right now does not come out of this number.@@Checked 2026-08-04 · Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Household Debt and Credit Report for Q1 2026, released 2026-05-12

@@CMP@@Schiff's reading|Delinquency is the highest since the aftermath of the crisis. Americans cannot pay their bills, which contradicts talk of a boom.|What the number shows|The level is high and has been parked there for five quarters. This is not deterioration in progress, it is a plateau at a high place.
The same 7% splits depending on whether you read its height or its slope.

## Counting money against counting people
Two different figures circulate for the same quarter.

TransUnion put credit card delinquency of 90 days or more at 2.5% for the first quarter of 2026, close to three times below the New York Fed figure.
Both are correct. They count different things.
The New York Fed measures overdue balances as a share of all card balances. TransUnion measures overdue borrowers as a share of all card borrowers.
People who fall behind tend to owe more, so counting by money produces a much larger share. Without checking which figure is on the table, two people can describe the same quarter in opposite terms.

@@REF@@US consumer credit market increasingly splitting along a K shaped path (TransUnion, 2026-04-30)|https://newsroom.transunion.com/k-shaped-q1-2026-ciir/|https://content.presspage.com/uploads/1104/47fd0a36-c08e-442c-b3af-546dd16c6101/1920_girl-holding-card-hand-paying-450w-2629574219.jpg?10000

## The top and the bottom are pulling apart
What TransUnion points at is not the average but the split.

The super prime tier grew to 40.7% of consumers by the fourth quarter of 2025, up 3.8 percentage points from the fourth quarter of 2019.
At the other end the subprime tier is growing and the middle is thinning out.
A flat headline delinquency rate can be the arithmetic of an improving top offsetting a deteriorating bottom.
One average line hides that motion. Schiff's sentence and any rebuttal that answers it with the average alone share the same blind spot.

Card balances themselves stand at $1.252 trillion, down $25 billion on the quarter and up $70 billion on the year.
The denominator under that percentage keeps growing.

## The August release of the Q2 report decides it
The next print settles this argument.

The New York Fed publishes the same report every quarter, and second quarter data lands within August.
A reading above 7.5% ends five quarters of flatness and hands the direction to Schiff. A reading below 7.5% means the plateau held.
Neither outcome changes the level, which is the highest stretch since 2011. Whether things are getting worse and whether they are already bad are separate questions, and today's data answers the second one.
trump-iran-strike-called-off-hormuz-deni:
President Trump has called off the planned US attack on Iran.
His stated reason was that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked him to hold off, and that the perimeters of a deal had been agreed.
That deal, he said, would include the immediate and complete opening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil fell about 5% within a day of the post.
West Texas Intermediate traded at $79.77 a barrel and Brent at $83.47.

@@REF@@Oil Prices Plunge 5% as Trump Halts Iran Strike Plans (OilPrice.com, 2026-08-02)|https://oilprice.com/Latest-Energy-News/World-News/Oil-Prices-Plunge-5-as-Trump-Halts-Iran-Strike-Plans.html|https://d32r1sh890xpii.cloudfront.net/news/1200x675/2026-08-02_8klqup39sh.jpg

The same report notes that the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency logged three more tanker attacks over the weekend.
Brent was under $72 at the start of July and closed above $90 last week, so this move gave back part of that run rather than all of it.

## Why one strait is this big

The Strait of Hormuz is the way out of the Persian Gulf into the Indian Ocean.
Crude loaded in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait and the UAE leaves through that single passage.

@@CHK@@Oil through Hormuz (2022 average)|21 million barrels a day|Share of world oil consumption|about 21%|Share of seaborne oil trade|more than a quarter@@This is why Trump put a complete opening, rather than anything else, at the front of the deal. A fifth of the oil the world burns leaves through this one channel. The figures date from 2022, when the strait ran normally, so actual flows under the current closure are lower.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · US Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy (published 2023-11-21, 2022 data)

Put simply, the strait behaves like a valve, not a dial.
It does not taper off. It either flows or it stops.
So a single sentence about who may pass moves the price 5% in a day.

## What exactly did Iran deny

Tehran tells it differently.
Iran's Mehr news agency said it never asked the US to hold off, and Fars said reports of an agreement to split control of the strait were false.

The official quoted by Fars attached conditions.
As long as the US continues what Iran calls hostile actions, the strait stays closed, and a ship may pass only along a route Iran designates and with permission from the Revolutionary Guards navy.

@@REF@@Iran denies it asked Trump not to strike or agreed to deal to split control of Hormuz (The Times of Israel, 2026-08-02)|https://www.timesofisrael.com/iran-denies-it-asked-trump-not-to-strike-or-agreed-to-deal-to-split-control-of-hormuz/|https://static-cdn.toi-media.com/www/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-02T091335Z_1478686883_MT1ANADL0007YG4ZC_RTRMADP_3_ANADOLU.jpg

The same report describes a compromise floated by Israel's Channel 12.
Ships would enter through Iranian-controlled water and leave through Omani water, and transit fees were reportedly left out of the outline.
Oman is said to have asked for assurances that the Guards would honour it.

@@CMP@@How the market read it|The attack is off and the strait is being opened. This is the point where the war premium comes out of the price.|How Iran's statement reads|There was no request and no deal. The strait stays shut until Washington backs off, and passage is something the Revolutionary Guards grant.

Both sides are describing the same two days, and they disagree on whether an agreement exists at all. What splits them is who sets the terms of passage.

## So what settles this

The question comes down to one thing.
Is this the start of the war premium unwinding, or a pause before it goes back on.

The place to look is the ships.
If tankers begin transiting without clearing it with the Revolutionary Guards first, the deal is working. If passage stays permission-based, the announcement was words.

Oil has already answered half of it. It gave up 5% and did not return to where it sat at the start of July.
The attack being cancelled is a confirmed fact. The strait being open is not one yet.
The market has priced itself somewhere in between.
kobeissi-q2-earnings-beat-record-ex-two-:
US companies are beating Q2 estimates by an unusual margin.
S&P 500 earnings have come in 31.4% above analyst estimates in aggregate, the widest gap since FactSet began tracking the figure in 2008.

The next passage of the same report carries a caveat.
Strip out Alphabet and Amazon and the number falls to 9.2%.

@@REF@@S&P 500 Earnings Season Update: July 31, 2026 (FactSet, 2026-07-31)|https://insight.factset.com/sp-500-earnings-season-update-july-31-2026|https://insight.factset.com/hubfs/1)Insight/Low%20Res%20Insight%20Headers/woman-executive-3.jpg

@@CHK@@S&P 500 companies reported|61%|Aggregate earnings surprise|+31.4%|Excluding Alphabet and Amazon|+9.2%@@The record itself is real. The same source also says the record came from non-operating gains at two companies, and that without them the surprise is 9.2%. That is still above the historical average, but it is a different claim from the strongest quarter in decades.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · FactSet Earnings Insight (2026-07-31, with 61% of the index reported)

## What happened at those two companies

Most of what those two booked was not money earned by selling anything.
It was the carrying value of stakes they already held moving up.

When an asset a company has not sold rises in value, accounting rules require that increase to be recorded as income in that quarter. That is an unrealised gain.
No cash arrives, and the net income line grows anyway.

A painting on your wall getting more valuable does not raise your salary that year. Corporate accounting still writes the increase into the profit line.

Amazon added $53.4 billion pre-tax to income this way from its Anthropic stake.
Operating income in the same quarter was $27.5 billion, so the mark-up on the stake was close to twice what the business itself earned.

@@REF@@Amazon's $200B Quarter: Ads, AWS, and the Anthropic Gain (Digital Applied, 2026-07-31)|https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/amazon-q2-2026-earnings-ads-aws-anthropic-gain|https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/amazon-q2-2026-earnings-ads-aws-anthropic-gain/article-image

Alphabet is the same shape.
As covered in an earlier card, Alphabet's pre-tax unrealised gain was $99 billion, from its SpaceX and Anthropic holdings.
Anthropic is the name that appears in both.

## So is the unprecedented AI earnings claim right

Half right.
Companies that converted AI demand into actual revenue, chipmakers and cloud operators, did post strong quarters again.

But that is not what produced the index-level surprise record.
What produced it was the book value of two companies' holdings in an AI startup.

@@CMP@@How Kobeissi reads it|AI-exposed companies are delivering unprecedented earnings, and a 27% aggregate beat is the evidence.|How the FactSet data reads|Most of the record is non-operating gains at Alphabet and Amazon. Take those out and it is 9.2%, high but not unprecedented.

Neither reading disputes that earnings are good. They split on whether the profit was earned by selling products or recorded because an AI company got more expensive on paper.

## So what settles this

The question comes down to one thing.
Is this record the size of the profit AI created, or the price someone put on an AI company.

The place to look is next quarter.
If Anthropic is not marked up again, this quarter's gain does not repeat, and if the valuation falls the same rule cuts net income in the other direction.
If the 9.2% ex-Alphabet-and-Amazon figure holds up next quarter, that supports the reading that AI demand is arriving as real revenue.

The record is a fact. Roughly two-thirds of what made it is the value of stakes nobody sold.
A number written in by a rule can be written out by the same rule.

Money is bet on SK hynix outside Korea too, through perpetual futures, contracts with no expiry. Nothing changes hands but the direction of the price, so a market can be opened anywhere, whether or not the stock is listed there.

One of the places these markets open is Hyperliquid. It is not an exchange run by a company with staff; it is a program written in advance that runs itself by fixed rules.

Whoever opens the market is a separate party. The SK hynix market was opened by trade.xyz, and trade.xyz also chose where the price would come from. It chose NextTrade.

## A seat that clears out on a 5% move

One of the rules trade.xyz set was 10x leverage: a million won of your own money carries a ten million won bet. Leverage comes with a maintenance margin line, and when equity falls below it the exchange does not wait, it closes the position on the spot. At 10x that line sits around 5%.

The reference price fell from $1,127.90 to $917.25, a drop of 18.7%.

A 5% line met an 18.7% move. There was only one outcome.

Hyperliquid said it provides the rails and that the party opening a market sets the price rules, BeInCrypto reported. The guard trade.xyz had set allowed a 10% move at once, plus one reset, for a maximum of 19%. The actual move stayed inside that band, so the guard worked as designed.

LPDDR is the low-power DRAM soldered directly onto the board of a phone or a laptop, and LPDDR6 is its newest generation.

TechTimes traces the gap to how the circuits get printed.
SK hynix prints in a single pass with extreme-ultraviolet tools at a 13.5 nanometer wavelength, while CXMT layers several passes with deep-ultraviolet tools at a longer wavelength.

Layering passes means aligning the plate again each time, and a little misalignment accumulates with every pass.
That accumulated error shaves the top speed the finished circuit can hold.
The ceiling gets cut off during the sorting step, where finished parts are binned by the speed they actually reach.

China has not been able to bring in a single extreme-ultraviolet tool.
So the 11% is less a question of CXMT's design skill than of access to equipment.

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether this is progress on the way to matching the standard, or a ceiling that stops just below its top.

The next generation settles it.
If 12,800 climbs to 14,400 within LPDDR6, multi-pass printing can reach the top after all, and if roughly the same 11% survives into the next generation, that is where the ceiling is.

Chinese memory has taken the route of entering on price and climbing toward the standard.
This number is the first time that road has been measured to the decimal.
It is also how the phrase "lithography is the last bottleneck" ends up written into a product spec sheet.

## Why did the won weaken while the surplus grew

Korea has been running its largest current account surplus on record this year.
The January to May total of $141.3 billion passed the $123 billion full-year surplus of 2025, itself a record, in five months.

And yet the rate was still above 1,550 in early July.

A current account surplus is an amount booked as earned. It is not a statement that those dollars came home.
When an exporter leaves the dollars it earned sitting in the US, the surplus grows and nothing is converted into won.

When a foreign investor sells Korean shares and leaves, the dollars going out are cash.
By the Bank of Korea's count, $110.2 billion left through equity sales between January and June.

Put simply, the ledger showed a surplus while dollars were walking out the door.

## What stopped

In the third week of July the foreign selling stopped.
This looks less like heavy buying than like fast-moving money pausing.
Once the cash stopped leaving, the surplus that had been piling up finally started to show in the rate.

Rates came in on top of that.

## What the government did

On the supply side, the authorities moved.

## Why the three sit in the same kind of seat

The three dissenters have something in common.
All are presidents of regional Reserve Banks, and none is a governor on the Federal Reserve Board.

The rate-setting committee seats seven governors nominated by the president alongside five regional presidents who rotate into a vote.
This time all seven governors voted to hold.

Put simply, the people inside the house agreed, and the disagreement came from those who visit it.
It also means the new chair managed to line up the governors behind him.

## The press conference is what changed

The more important part of the day was not the vote but the press conference.
Chair Kevin Warsh's thinking fits into one line.

If the Fed does not pre-announce its decisions or hint at direction, markets will price their own read of the economy rather than the Fed's words.

That is a decision not to give forward guidance.
Forward guidance means the central bank telling you in advance what it intends to do with rates.
Ben Bernanke reached for it in 2008, when the rate could not go lower, as a way of pulling future cheap money into the present.

Since then the chair's press conference after each meeting has been where you read the next move.
Take that away and there is less reason to listen.

## What changes for markets

Remove the pre-announcement and the raw material for prices changes.
Until now the chair's words came first and the data confirmed them. Now the data comes first and the market has to interpret it alone.

The same print leaves more room for disagreement, which means bigger moves on the days data lands.
Forbes notes that Bank of America expects three quarter-point hikes this year.
With no guidance to check it against, a forecast like that gets priced as guesswork rather than confirmation.

## So what will tell us which it was

In the end the question is one.
Whether removing the pre-announcement is a normalisation that pushes markets back to the data, or a retreat that only adds volatility.

The place to look is what happens on data days.
If rate futures swing harder than they used to when inflation or jobs numbers land, the cushion guidance used to provide is gone.
If instead the stretches between meetings get quieter, markets really have started pricing the economy rather than the chair.

The 9-3 vote will matter less over time than the decision to stop talking.
The rate did not move, but the way you read the rate did.

The US personal consumption expenditures price index fell 0.1% in June from the month before.
That is the first monthly decline in this index in six years.

Against a year earlier it ran 3.7%, down from 4.1% in May.
The biggest single mover was energy goods, including gasoline, which fell 9.2%.

@@REF@@Inflation rate fell by 0.1% in June, first decrease in six years (UPI, 2026-07-30)|https://www.upi.com/Top_News/US/2026/07/30/personal-consumption-expenditures-june-2026/4151785423293/|https://cdnph.upi.com/sv/ph/og/upi/4151785423293/2026/1/6002c295230d40502dff7b0b8abb84de/v1.5/Inflation-rate-fell-by-01-in-June-first-decrease-in-six-years.jpg

UPI reports that the 9.2% drop in energy goods was the largest since August 2022.
What pushed the index negative for a month, in other words, was energy rather than prices in general.

The reason markets cheered the number sits two days earlier, at the Fed meeting.
Rates were held 9 to 3, and all three dissents were for a hike rather than a cut.
Data showing prices cooling takes the wind out of the side arguing for higher rates.

## Why the Fed does not watch the CPI

Here is the part that snags.
The number we call inflation in the news is usually the consumer price index, the CPI.
But the yardstick the Fed measures its 2% target against is not the CPI. It is the personal consumption expenditures price index, the PCE.

The two are built differently.
The CPI fixes more than a hundred thousand items into a basket and prices that basket.
The PCE keeps changing what is in the basket according to what people actually bought.

When beef gets expensive, households buy more chicken.
A fixed basket cannot follow that move, so it charges the full beef increase to the index.
That failure to see shoppers switching to whatever got cheaper, which makes measured inflation run high, is called substitution bias.

## Why this statistic was a political problem

The homework in front of Congress in 1995 was the deficit.
More than half of federal spending was mandatory, programs like Social Security, and both those increases and the income tax brackets were indexed to the CPI.

Indexed means one CPI print moves spending and tax revenue at the same time.
So a finding that the CPI overstated inflation changed the arithmetic.
It would slow the growth of outlays without anyone having to vote to cut pensions.

The commission Congress set up delivered its verdict on December 4, 1996.
The CPI was overstating inflation by about 1.1 percentage points a year, and substitution bias was the largest single piece of it.

@@REF@@Final Report of the Advisory Commission to Study the Consumer Price Index (US Social Security Administration archive, 1996-12-04)|https://www.ssa.gov/history/reports/boskinrpt.html

The report itself spells out why a statistic was a money question.
If the CPI overstated the cost of living by one percentage point a year for a decade, the report calculated, the resulting addition to the deficit would reach roughly $135 billion by 2006, making it the fourth largest federal program behind Social Security, health care and defense.

The Fed's official yardstick changed from CPI to PCE in February 2000.

## Does that yardstick really read lower

That holds as a long-run average, but June ran the other way. Energy prices fell hard, and energy carries more weight in the CPI, so the CPI came down further. Strip out food and energy and the gap widens to 0.7 points in the same direction. For this month alone, the number the Fed uses was the stricter one, not the softer one.@@Retrieved 2026-07-31 · US Bureau of Labor Statistics June CPI (released 2026-07-17) · US Bureau of Economic Analysis June PCE (released 2026-07-30)

The effect of swapping yardsticks is not the kind of thing a single month confirms.
Averages running lower and this month running lower are different claims, and this month was inverted.

## How we will know

In the end there is one question.
Is this cooling the start of a trend, or a one month energy effect.

The place it splits is oil.
What pulled June down was the drop in crude that came out of a temporary truce with Iran, and in July that truce broke and crude is rising again.
If energy turns positive again in the July print, June was a one month affair. If core prices, with food and energy stripped out, keep coming down alongside it, the trend reading holds.

The side that changed the yardstick and the side that asked for the change each had their own arithmetic.
The Fed got a target that is easier to hit, and Congress got a way to shrink the deficit without losing votes.
It is worth knowing how the number markets are cheering today was chosen.

## Why only the borrowed part moved

When you post collateral with a broker and borrow to buy stock, a falling price leaves that collateral short.
The broker then asks you to top it up, and if you cannot, the broker sells for you.
That is a margin call, and the party holding the collateral is the prime broker.

Situational Awareness is reported to have run about four times leverage on its listed book.
Four times means one part your own money and three parts borrowed, buying four.
At that ratio a 25% fall in the stock produces a loss of one, which is exactly all of your own money.

In July the names the fund held fell between 35% and 47%.
That is far past 25%, so on the arithmetic the equity behind the listed book was already gone.
